title: A Loan Has a Price and a Structure, and the Structure Matters More
summary: Every loan offer has price terms, such as the rate and fees, and structure terms, such as leverage, recourse, covenants and reserves. Price decides your return in a good year; structure decides whether you survive a bad one. Priya sets out what to ask for, what to trade and when to walk away from a lender.
body:
The interest rate is the term everyone negotiates and the one that matters least in a bad year. What decides whether you survive a downturn is the structure: how much is borrowed, who guarantees it, what tests it must pass and what happens to your cash when it fails one.

Recall

Q. What does writing subject to contract on a negotiating email do?

A. It signals that you do not intend to be bound until a final agreement is signed, which helps stop an exchange of emails being treated as a contract. It is strong evidence of intent, not an absolute guarantee.

Q. In the Six-Lens Check, which lens asks whether a lender can follow the cash?

A. The banking lens. It asks whether money moves through the structure in a way a lender can see, secure and rely on, and where it could be trapped or delayed.

Q. Why does the distinction between active and passive income matter for a foreign affiliate?

A. Because many countries tax passive income earned in a controlled foreign company in the owner’s hands as it is earned, while active business income may be deferred. The tests and rules vary; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, last week was negotiation in general. This week we take it to the one counterparty you will negotiate with most often and depend on most heavily: the lender. A developer who fights only on rate wins a few basis points and loses his house in the next recession. A developer who understands structure gives a little on price to buy room to breathe, and that room is what keeps a project alive when rents stall or rates jump.

A basis point is one hundredth of a percentage point, so 25 basis points is 0.25 percent. Lenders talk in them, so you should too.

Price terms and structure terms

In plain English: price terms are what the loan costs if everything goes to plan. Structure terms are what the loan does to you when things go wrong.

The professional framing sorts a term sheet into two lists. Price: interest rate or spread over a benchmark, upfront fee, exit fee, and the cost of any required hedge. Structure: loan amount and the limit that sizes it (debt service coverage ratio, loan to value, loan to cost or debt yield, from Week 36), recourse and guarantees, financial covenants and how often they are tested, reserves, cash management, prepayment terms, and conditions to funding.

Two structure terms deserve names today. A cash sweep is a clause that diverts all or part of the property’s surplus cash to the lender, to pay down the loan or to hold in a reserve, when a test such as the coverage ratio falls below a set level. A prepayment premium is a charge for repaying the loan early, sometimes a flat percentage and sometimes a formula designed to give the lender the interest it would have earned. Both are commercial terms, negotiated deal by deal.

What to ask for

Ask first for the terms that protect you in the bad year, and only then for price. A practical order: recourse limited and capped, with a clear end date; covenants with headroom and a cure right, meaning the right to fix a breach by depositing cash or paying down the loan; a cash sweep that switches off when the ratio recovers; prepayment flexibility that matches your exit plan; and conditions to funding that you can actually control.

A worked example, with hypothetical round numbers. A building earns net operating income (NOI) of 2,000,000 dollars. Annual debt service is 1,500,000 dollars, so the coverage ratio is 1.33. Lender A sets the covenant at 1.30; Lender B at 1.20. Under A, NOI can fall to 1,950,000 dollars before you breach: a fall of 2.5 percent. Under B, NOI can fall to 1,800,000 dollars: a fall of 10 percent. A single bad tenant or a property tax increase can cost 2.5 percent. That difference in headroom is worth more than a quarter point of rate in most years you will ever live through.

Say that out loud now.

What to trade, and when to walk

Trade what is cheap for you and valuable to the lender, as JAX taught last week. Lenders value fees paid at closing, deposits held with them, more equity in first, a longer lock-out period if you do not plan to sell early, and good information: monthly reporting, budget approval rights, an independent monitor. You can often give these without changing your risk.

Be careful trading the other way. A lower rate in exchange for full personal recourse, a tighter covenant or a floating rate with no cap moves risk from the lender to you. Sometimes that is worth it. Price it first, which Roman will do on Day 3.

When to walk: when the binding sizing limit leaves a gap you cannot fill with equity you actually have; when the covenants would be breached on day one or under a mild downside; when the lender insists on recourse you cannot carry; or when the lender reserves the right to change terms late without limits. A second worked example: you need 20,000,000 dollars to make the deal work. The best lender, on its own coverage test, will lend 19,000,000 dollars. You have no more equity. The honest answer is not to accept a riskier loan from someone else to fill the gap. It is to restructure the deal or walk.

How the best do it

Experienced institutional sponsors rarely ask one lender for a quote. They run a competitive process: a short information package, several lenders invited to bid, and every term sheet entered into a comparison grid with price and structure side by side. They negotiate structure before price, and they pick the lender with the best combination of terms and reliability, not only the lowest rate. A small developer can copy this with a spreadsheet and three phone calls. The grid alone stops you from comparing rates while ignoring recourse.

Six-Lens Check

Tax. Interest deductibility, fees and any hedge payments have tax treatment that differs by country; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Liability. Recourse and guarantees decide whether a project loss becomes a personal one; cap them and give them an end date.

Banking. The relationship outlasts one loan; a lender who sees honest reporting through a bad year will lend again.

Governance. Decide who may sign loan documents and give guarantees, and record it in a resolution before closing.

Estate. A personal guarantee can outlive you and bind your estate; record every one where your executor will find it.

Exit. Prepayment terms decide whether you can sell or refinance when the market is right; match them to the exit plan.

A one-page lender brief

Before you call any lender, write one page: the building, its income, the loan you need, the limit you expect to bind, the structure terms you will not give, and your alternative. Send the same page to every lender, so their bids answer the same question and your grid compares like with like.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is choosing a loan on rate alone and accepting structure terms that break the project in an ordinary downturn. The control is a comparison grid with every term in it, and a rule that structure is negotiated before price.

The beginner's mistake

Treating the lender’s first term sheet as standard. It is an opening position. Covenant levels, recourse caps, sweep triggers and prepayment terms all move, but only if you ask.

Callback

In Week 36, Priya taught sizing a loan to the binding limit. Today adds the other half: the limit sets how much you can borrow, and the covenants set how much the building can fall before the loan turns against you. Size to the limit, then test the headroom.

Recap

A loan has price terms and structure terms, and structure decides survival. Ask for limited recourse, covenant headroom, cure rights, a sweep that switches off and prepayment that fits your exit. Trade fees, information and equity, not personal exposure, unless you have priced it. Walk when the gap cannot be filled honestly.

Next: Ford, with Roman, on Failure Forensics: a lower rate that cost a family its savings.
checklist: I have split every term sheet into price terms and structure terms.
I negotiated structure before I negotiated price.
I computed the covenant headroom as a percentage fall in NOI.
I asked for a cure right and a sweep that switches off when the ratio recovers.
I matched prepayment terms to my exit plan.
I entered every offer into one comparison grid.
I know the funding gap I can fill with equity I actually have.
Every guarantee I would give is capped and has an end date.
head: Field checklist
speak: A loan has a price and a structure. The price is the rate and fees. The structure is how much I borrow and what sizes it, who guarantees it, which covenants it must pass and how often, what reserves it holds, what happens to my cash when a test fails, and what it costs to repay early. Price decides my return in a good year; structure decides whether I survive a bad one. So I negotiate structure first: limited and capped recourse with an end date, covenants with headroom and a cure right, a cash sweep that switches off when the ratio recovers, and prepayment terms that match my exit. I trade things that are cheap for me and valuable to the lender, such as fees, reporting and equity in first. I put every offer in a comparison grid. And I walk away when the gap between what the lender will lend and what the deal needs is bigger than the equity I really have.
terms: Cash sweep — a clause that diverts a property’s surplus cash to the lender when a test such as the coverage ratio falls below a set level.
Prepayment premium — a charge for repaying a loan before its term ends, negotiated as a percentage or a formula.
Cure right — the borrower’s right to fix a covenant breach, usually by depositing cash or paying down the loan, before it becomes a default.

hostile.q: Our rate is the best you will find. Why are you spending time on covenant levels and recourse instead of signing?
hostile.a: Because the rate matters most when things go well, and the covenants and recourse matter most when they do not. At your 1.30 covenant this building can lose 2.5 percent of its income before we breach; at 1.20 it can lose 10 percent. I would happily pay a little more in fees or give you monthly reporting to get that headroom. I want a loan we both still like in a bad year.

title: The Cheaper Loan That Cost the House
summary: This is a composite example. A developer took the lowest rate on offer and in exchange gave full personal recourse, a tight coverage covenant and an unhedged floating rate. When rates rose, the covenant broke, the cash sweep starved the property and the guarantee was called. Ford and Roman take it apart.
rule: Rule 67: Never trade structure for price until you have priced the downside; a lower rate is not worth wider recourse, a tighter covenant or an unhedged floating rate unless its saving is larger than the expected cost of the bad case.
body:
This is a composite example. A developer saved a fraction of a percent on his interest rate and paid for it with full personal recourse, a covenant with almost no headroom and a floating rate with no cap. Two years later, rising rates did the rest.

Recall

Q. How do you derive a walk-away land price?

A. Fix your required yield on cost, divide the stabilised net operating income by it to find the most the project can cost, and subtract all non-land costs. What remains is the most you can pay for land.

Q. At a checkpoint, why is a structure that saves tax but cannot show substance a failure?

A. Because an authority can disregard or recharacterise arrangements that lack real substance, and then the saving disappears and penalties may follow. The structure must match what actually happens.

Q. What usually triggers controlled-foreign-company rules?

A. Control of a foreign company by residents, combined with income of a passive or mobile type. The thresholds and definitions differ by country; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Roman joins me because this case is about the translation of a project problem into a personal one. Nothing here is unusual. Every term was offered by a reputable lender and accepted by a competent developer who was trying to save money. That is exactly why it is worth studying: the trap is built from ordinary choices.

1. Timeline

All figures are hypothetical. A developer completed a 100-unit apartment building and sought a 20,000,000 dollar loan to repay construction debt. Two lenders bid. Lender A offered a floating rate 0.35 percentage points below Lender B, with full personal recourse, a debt service coverage ratio covenant of 1.30 tested quarterly, and a cash sweep of all surplus cash below that level. Lender B offered a slightly higher fixed rate, recourse capped at a quarter of the loan, and a 1.20 covenant. The developer chose Lender A to save about 70,000 dollars a year.

In year one, coverage was about 1.38. In year two, the benchmark rate rose sharply. Debt service rose with it, and coverage fell to 1.25, then 1.18. The sweep began; every surplus dollar went to the lender. Repairs were deferred, vacancy rose, and coverage fell further. In year three the lender declared a default after the cure period passed and demanded payment under the guarantee. The developer sold personal investments and his family home to settle.

2. Key decisions

Three decisions carried the weight: choosing a floating rate with no cap or hedge, accepting a covenant with only 0.08 of headroom over actual coverage, and giving full personal recourse to buy a small rate saving.

3. Assumptions

The developer assumed rates would stay near their current level, that the building’s income would keep growing, that the sweep would never bite, and that a lender would refinance him before trouble arrived. He also assumed the saving was certain while the risks were unlikely, which is true in most years and false in the one that matters.

Say that out loud now.

4. Incentives

The developer’s partner was paid on cash flow this year, so a lower rate looked like money in the pocket. The broker was paid a fee on closing, whichever loan was chosen. The lender priced the full recourse as protection and offered a better rate for it. Nobody in the room was paid to model the bad year.

5. Warning signs ignored

The covenant headroom was tiny: coverage could fall by less than 6 percent before breaching, and a quarter point rise in the benchmark would take most of that. The forward market for interest rates was already pricing increases, which a hedge quote would have revealed. The developer’s own household had no reserve outside the project to cure a breach. And the guarantee had no cap and no end date, which meant it would last for the life of the loan.

6. Point of no return

The point of no return was the start of the cash sweep. Once surplus cash went to the lender, the property could not fund repairs or leasing, income fell, and coverage fell further. A sweep that cannot be cured becomes a spiral. Before that point, the developer could have bought an interest rate cap or paid down the loan to restore headroom. After it, his options were the lender’s.

7. Root cause

The root cause was trading structure for price without pricing the downside. The saving was about 70,000 dollars a year. The bad case, a call on a 20,000,000 dollar guarantee, did not need to be likely to outweigh that saving many times over.

Roman's view: pricing the trade they did not price

Roman here. A worked example, hypothetical. Suppose the developer had judged a 5 percent chance, over the loan term, that the guarantee would be called, and that the loss on a call would be 30 percent of the loan, or 6,000,000 dollars. The expected cost is 5 percent of 6,000,000 dollars, which is 300,000 dollars. Against that, Lender B’s capped recourse would have limited the exposure to 5,000,000 dollars and, under the same assumptions, a loss of at most 1,500,000 dollars, an expected cost of 75,000 dollars. The difference, 225,000 dollars, is larger than three years of the rate saving. And that ignores the loss of the family home, which no expected-value sum captures.

A second worked example: the interest rate cap. A cap is a contract that pays you when a floating benchmark rises above a set level, so your borrowing cost stops rising. Its price varies with the market and the term. Had the developer asked for a quote at closing and found that it cost a fraction of the first year’s saving, he would have seen at once that the cheap loan was only cheap without protection.

What a disciplined borrower would have done

Ford again. Five steps, none of them clever. First, put both offers in a grid with every term priced, as Roman will show tomorrow. Second, ask for a quote for an interest rate cap on the floating offer and add its cost to the rate before comparing. Third, compute covenant headroom as a percentage fall in income and test it against a one-point rise in the benchmark; here, a one-point rise alone would have broken the covenant. Fourth, refuse uncapped recourse, or accept it only with a burn-off, meaning a clause that ends or reduces the guarantee when the building reaches a stated level of coverage for a stated period. Fifth, keep a household reserve outside the project equal to at least one cure payment.

A worked example of the cure, hypothetical. Coverage falls to 1.25 against a 1.30 covenant on debt service of 1,450,000 dollars. To restore 1.30 on current income of about 1,812,000 dollars, debt service must fall to about 1,394,000 dollars. On an interest-only basis at 7 percent, that means repaying about 800,000 dollars of loan. A developer with 800,000 dollars set aside cures and survives. A developer without it watches the sweep begin.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is accepting personal recourse and tight covenants as the price of a lower rate. The control is Rule 67: price the downside of every structure term before you accept it in exchange for price.

The beginner's mistake

Reading the comparison grid row by row and choosing the lowest rate, instead of asking which loan you would rather have in the worst year of its term.

Callback

In Week 46, Ford and Roman studied leverage spirals and guarantee calls. This case shows the mechanism inside a single building: the sweep that removes the cash needed to recover. Recognise a sweep without a realistic cure as the start of a spiral, not as a protection.

Recap

A composite developer saved about 70,000 dollars a year and accepted full recourse, a tight covenant and an unhedged floating rate. Rates rose, the covenant broke, the sweep starved the property and the guarantee was called. Rule 67: never trade structure for price until you have priced the downside.

Next: Roman on The Money: putting a dollar value on every loan term.
checklist: I priced the expected cost of each structure term I am asked to accept.
I compared any rate saving with that expected cost over the full term.
I asked for a hedge or cap quote before choosing a floating rate.
I computed covenant headroom and tested it against a rate rise.
I know how the cash sweep works and how it switches off.
I hold a reserve outside the project able to cure a breach.
Every guarantee is capped and has an end date.
head: Field checklist
speak: This is a composite example. A developer refinancing a 100-unit building chose the cheapest loan, saving about 70,000 dollars a year. In exchange he accepted a floating rate with no cap, a coverage covenant of 1.30 against actual coverage of 1.38, a sweep of all surplus cash on breach, and full personal recourse. Rates rose. Coverage fell to 1.18, the sweep took every surplus dollar, repairs stopped, income fell further, and the lender called the guarantee. He sold his family home. The root cause was trading structure for price without pricing the downside. Even a small chance of a guarantee call on a 20,000,000 dollar loan carries an expected cost larger than years of the saving, and that is before counting a home. Rule 67: never trade structure for price until you have priced the downside, and never accept a sweep without a realistic way to cure it.
terms: Interest rate cap — a contract that pays the borrower when a floating benchmark rises above a set level, limiting the cost of borrowing.
Covenant headroom — how far income or value can fall before a financial covenant is breached, best expressed as a percentage.
Full recourse — a lender’s right to recover the whole loan from the borrower or guarantor personally, not just from the property.

hostile.q: The other lender offered you a better rate. Why are you taking ours at a higher cost?
hostile.a: Because I priced the whole offer, not just the rate. Their saving was about 70,000 dollars a year. Their structure meant full personal recourse, a covenant that would break with a small rate rise and a sweep with no realistic cure. When I price the chance of that going wrong, the expected cost is larger than the saving. Your loan costs a little more and lets the building survive a bad year, which is better for both of us.

title: Putting a Dollar Value on Every Loan Term
summary: Two term sheets with different rates, fees, recourse and prepayment terms can only be compared once each term is turned into dollars. Roman computes the all-in cost, the expected cost of recourse and of prepayment premiums, and the cost of a cash sweep, using hypothetical numbers.
body:
You cannot compare two loans by their rates. Turn every term into dollars, the fees into an annual cost, and recourse and prepayment into expected costs, and the cheaper loan is often the one with the higher rate.

Recall

Q. What should you do immediately after you state your number in a landowner meeting?

A. Stay silent and let the other side speak next; filling the silence with justifications or small concessions gives away ground for nothing.

Q. How is leakage measured in a structure defence?

A. Layer by layer: the tax, withholding and costs lost each time cash moves up the structure, added together to show what reaches the owners.

Q. In concept, why can passive income in a controlled foreign company be taxed before it is distributed?

A. Because some countries treat that income as earned by the resident owners as it arises, to stop income being parked offshore. The rules vary; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Priya told you on Day 1 to negotiate structure before price. Ford showed what happens when that is ignored. My job today is to give you the arithmetic, so that when a lender says its rate is lower, you can answer with a number rather than a feeling. All figures are hypothetical; the probabilities are judgments you must make and write down.

The two offers

You need a 20,000,000 dollar loan and expect to hold the building for three years. Lender A offers 6.25 percent interest, a 1.0 percent upfront fee, full personal recourse, a cash sweep below a 1.30 coverage ratio, and a 2 percent prepayment premium in years one and two. Lender B offers 6.60 percent, a 0.5 percent fee, recourse capped at 5,000,000 dollars, a sweep below 1.20, and a 1 percent premium in year one only.

Step 1: the all-in cost of price terms

Spread the upfront fee over the expected hold. Lender A’s fee is 1.0 percent over three years, about 0.33 percent a year, so its all-in rate is about 6.58 percent. Lender B’s fee is 0.5 percent over three years, about 0.17 percent a year, so its all-in rate is about 6.77 percent. Lender A is cheaper by about 0.19 percent a year, roughly 38,000 dollars a year on 20,000,000 dollars, or about 114,000 dollars over three years. This is the number the lender will point to.

Step 2: the expected cost of recourse

Lender A exposes you to the full 20,000,000 dollars; Lender B to 5,000,000 dollars. The extra exposure is 15,000,000 dollars. Suppose you judge a 3 percent chance, over the three years, of a guarantee call, and a loss of 40 percent of the exposed amount if it happens. The expected cost of the extra exposure is 3 percent of 40 percent of 15,000,000 dollars, which is 180,000 dollars. Already Lender A’s saving is gone.

Say that out loud now.

Step 3: prepayment and the sweep

Suppose there is a 40 percent chance you sell in year two. Lender A’s premium then is 2 percent of 20,000,000 dollars, or 400,000 dollars, an expected cost of 160,000 dollars. Lender B has no premium in year two, so its expected cost is zero. If the sale might come in year one instead, run that case too.

The sweep is smaller but real. Suppose a 30 percent chance that coverage dips below 1.30 for a year under Lender A, trapping 300,000 dollars of surplus cash that you could otherwise use at a 10 percent return. The cost is about 30,000 dollars if it happens, an expected 9,000 dollars. Lender B’s lower trigger makes that case much less likely; treat it as near zero.

Step 4: add it up

Lender A is cheaper on price by about 114,000 dollars. It is more expensive on recourse by about 180,000 dollars, on prepayment by about 160,000 dollars and on the sweep by about 9,000 dollars. Net, Lender B is better by roughly 235,000 dollars in expected terms, before you count the value of sleeping at night. Change the probabilities and the answer may change, which is why you write them down and test them: at what chance of a guarantee call does Lender A become worth it? Here, almost never.

A second worked example, the other direction. If you are certain to hold for ten years, the fee spreads over more years and the prepayment premium becomes irrelevant. Run the same steps and Lender A’s rate advantage grows. The point is not that the higher rate always wins. It is that you only know which wins after every term is in dollars.

Warrick's Wealth Ledger

Warrick here. On your personal balance sheet, a guarantee is a contingent liability, and lenders and your own future self will look at the total. Keep a schedule: every guarantee, its cap, its trigger, its end date and the asset it would hit. A household with three uncapped guarantees on three buildings is not diversified; it is one recession away from a single loss. A licensed adviser is required before you act on any personal financial decision.

A third worked example: the cost of a reserve the lender holds

Lender B also asks you to fund a 600,000 dollar replacement reserve at closing, held by the lender and earning nothing, released when the building reaches a coverage of 1.40 for two quarters. If you expect the release after two years and your money otherwise earns 10 percent, the reserve costs you about 600,000 times 10 percent times two years, roughly 120,000 dollars of lost return, less anything the account pays you. That is a real cost and belongs in the grid. It does not change today’s answer, because Lender B was ahead by about 235,000 dollars, but it narrows the gap to about 115,000 dollars. Ask for the reserve to earn interest, to be released earlier, or to be smaller. Each of those requests now has a dollar value you can state.

Keep the grid honest

Three habits keep this arithmetic useful. Use the same hold period and the same discount rate for every offer. Write each probability next to the line it drives, with one sentence on how you chose it. And ask a second person, ideally one who wants the cheaper loan, to challenge each probability. If your answer only holds when the probabilities are generous to your preferred lender, it is not an answer yet.

Turning the grid into a negotiation

Now use the numbers. Go back to Lender A and say: “Your rate is better, but your recourse and prepayment terms cost us about 340,000 dollars in expected terms over the hold. If you cap recourse at 5,000,000 dollars and drop the year-two premium, you win.” You have given the lender a precise target, and you have shown that you are not choosing on rate alone. Lenders respond to a borrower who can price their terms, because it tells them which concessions will actually win the deal.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is comparing loans on headline rate and treating structure as free. The control is a grid that converts every term to dollars, with your probabilities written beside each line.

The beginner's mistake

Forgetting the expected hold period. A fee or a prepayment premium that is trivial over ten years can decide the comparison over three.

Callback

In Week 44, Roman taught break-evens and stress tests. The question at the end of Step 4 is a break-even: the probability at which the two loans cost the same. Find that number and ask whether you really believe the true probability is below it.

Recap

Spread fees over the expected hold to get the all-in rate. Price recourse, prepayment and sweeps as expected costs. Add them up and test the probabilities. Record every guarantee on your personal ledger.

Next: LEX on The Rules: term sheets, commitment letters and what the loan agreement really binds.
checklist: I spread every fee over my expected hold to find the all-in rate.
I priced the extra recourse as an expected cost.
I priced prepayment premiums against the chance of an early sale.
I priced the cash sweep as trapped cash at my opportunity cost.
I added every term into one net comparison.
I found the break-even probability that makes the two loans equal.
My personal guarantee schedule is up to date.
head: Field checklist
speak: I never compare loans by rate alone. First I spread the fees over my expected hold: on a three-year hold, a 1 percent fee adds about a third of a percent a year. Here that made Lender A cheaper by about 114,000 dollars. Then I price the structure. Lender A’s full recourse adds 15,000,000 dollars of exposure; at a 3 percent chance of a call and a 40 percent loss, that is an expected 180,000 dollars. Its prepayment premium, with a 40 percent chance I sell in year two, is another 160,000 dollars. Its tighter sweep adds a little more. Net, the higher-rate Lender B is better by about 235,000 dollars. The probabilities are my judgments, so I write them down and find the break-even. And I keep every guarantee on my personal ledger, because uncapped guarantees on several buildings turn one bad year into a single personal loss.
terms: All-in rate — the interest rate plus fees spread over the expected holding period, used to compare loans on price.
Expected hold — the period you realistically expect to keep the loan, which decides how fees and premiums should be spread.
Break-even probability — the chance of a bad outcome at which two options cost the same in expected terms.

hostile.q: Your probabilities are invented. Why should our credit committee care about them?
hostile.a: They are judgments, not inventions, and I have written down how I reached each one. Your committee will make its own. The point is that we are both pricing the same risks. If your committee believes the chance of a guarantee call is near zero, then capping recourse costs you very little, and I would ask you to agree to it on that basis.

title: Term Sheet, Commitment Letter, Loan Agreement: What Binds and When
summary: A lender’s promise grows in stages, from a non-binding term sheet to a commitment letter to the loan agreement and security. LEX explains what each stage binds, how conditions and discretion clauses work, and, in Two Systems, how Canada and Guyana approach lender security in concept. Verify all of it against primary sources.
body:
A lender’s yes comes in stages, and only the last stage is a promise you can rely on. Know what each document binds, who has discretion in it, and what happens if a condition is not met, and you will never mistake a term sheet for money.

Recall

Q. What is the zone of possible agreement?

A. The range between the two sides’ reservation prices, inside which any deal leaves both better off than walking away.

Q. In a checkpoint defence of a structure, what is the rules seat’s main question?

A. Whether each step has a legal basis that matches what actually happens, and whether anti-avoidance rules could disregard it.

Q. What reporting duty commonly comes with owning a foreign affiliate?

A. An information return disclosing the affiliate and its income, often with penalties for late filing. The forms and thresholds vary; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, developers lose deals between the term sheet and the funding, usually because they treated an early document as a commitment and spent money or signed a land contract on the strength of it. This lesson is concepts, not advice. Lending law varies by country and, in Canada, by province. Verify every point against the primary source before you rely on it.

Three stages of a lender’s promise

In plain English: the term sheet says what the lender is thinking, the commitment letter says what it will do if conditions are met, and the loan agreement is the deal itself.

The professional framing. A term sheet is usually expressly non-binding on the main terms, though it may bind you on a fee, exclusivity or costs. A commitment letter is usually a binding offer by the lender to lend on stated terms, subject to conditions precedent: events that must happen before the lender must fund, such as a satisfactory appraisal, title, insurance, legal opinions and no material adverse change. The loan agreement and the security documents are the binding contract and the lender’s rights over the property.

A worked example, hypothetical. You sign a term sheet for 20,000,000 dollars and, relying on it, waive the financing condition in your land purchase. The lender’s credit committee then cuts the loan to 18,000,000 dollars. The term sheet said it was non-binding and subject to credit approval. You are now bound to buy land with a 2,000,000 dollar gap. The control: never waive a financing condition on a term sheet; at the earliest, waive it on a commitment letter whose conditions you can meet.

Conditions, discretion and material adverse change

Read every condition precedent and ask two questions: who decides whether it is met, and is that decision objective or discretionary? A condition that an appraisal shows value of at least a stated figure is objective. A condition that the lender is satisfied in its sole discretion with the borrower’s financial condition is not; it can let a lender walk away for almost any reason. Courts in some places read limits into discretion, but do not rely on that.

A material adverse change clause lets a lender refuse to fund if something seriously damages the borrower, the property or sometimes the market. Ask for it to be limited to the borrower and the property, not the general market, because a market downturn is exactly when you most need the money you were promised.

Say that out loud now.

Covenants, defaults and cross-default

Once the loan funds, the agreement binds you through covenants: financial ones, such as coverage ratios, and operating ones, such as keeping insurance and not selling or borrowing more without consent. Breaching a covenant can be an event of default, which you met in Week 39. Ask for notice and a cure period before default. Watch for cross-default: a clause that makes a default under another loan, sometimes any loan of yours or your affiliates, a default under this one. One troubled building can then put every loan in your group at risk.

A second worked example. You have loans on three buildings with different lenders. Building one breaches a covenant. Loans two and three contain cross-default clauses referring to any indebtedness of the guarantor. All three lenders now have default rights at once. Ask for cross-default to be limited to the same borrower and above a meaningful threshold.

Two Systems: lender security in Canada and Guyana

Conceptually, and flagged verify against primary source. In Canada, real property security is registered under provincial land registration systems, and personal property security is governed by provincial statutes in the common-law provinces, with Quebec following its civil law code; enforcement of a mortgage may proceed by power of sale or judicial process depending on the province. Federal statutes also touch lending, for example on interest disclosure. Guyana’s legal system draws on English common law, while its land law carries a Roman-Dutch heritage, and mortgages and transports of land are recorded through its deeds and land registries; enforcement generally involves the courts [unverified — confirm independently]. The practical point is the same in both: what protects a lender, and therefore what it will ask of you, is registered security and an enforcement route it trusts. Verify against primary source before relying on any of this.

Representations and the borrower’s certificate

The loan agreement also contains representations: statements of fact by you, such as that the rent roll is accurate, there is no litigation and the financial statements are true. Many loans require you to repeat them at each draw or each reporting date. A false representation can be an event of default even if nothing else has gone wrong. A third worked example, hypothetical: your rent roll shows a 10,000 dollar monthly tenant who gave notice last week. You certify the rent roll as accurate. If the lender later finds the notice, you have made a false representation, and the default may be immediate. The control is simple. Before you sign any certificate, update every schedule it refers to and keep the evidence on file.

Personal guarantees as separate contracts

A guarantee is usually a separate document from the loan agreement, and it can survive changes to the loan. Read whether changes to the loan, such as an extension or an increase, need your consent as guarantor, and whether the guarantee covers only this loan or all your obligations to that lender. An all-obligations guarantee can make you liable for loans you never meant to support.

Keep a copy of every guarantee you have signed in one place, with the lender, the cap and the end date on the first page.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is treating a term sheet or a commitment with discretionary conditions as committed money, and binding yourself to a purchase on that basis. The control is to keep your own financing condition until the lender’s remaining conditions are objective and within your control.

The beginner's mistake

Reading only the economic terms of a commitment letter and skipping the conditions precedent and the cross-default clause, which decide whether the money arrives and how far a problem spreads.

Callback

In Week 20, LEX taught formation, conditions and what binds in letters of intent and term sheets. The same tests apply to the lender: essential terms agreed, intention to be bound, and conditions that are certain enough to enforce. A lender’s term sheet is a letter of intent wearing a bank’s logo. Professional sign-off required: a lawyer qualified in the governing law, before you sign a commitment letter or loan agreement.

Recap

Term sheets rarely bind on the loan; commitment letters bind subject to conditions; the loan agreement and security bind fully. Read who decides each condition, narrow material adverse change, ask for cure periods, and limit cross-default. Both Canada and Guyana protect lenders through registered security, so expect lenders to ask for it.

Next: Priya on The Numbers: sizing a loan, testing its headroom and finding the walk-away point.
checklist: I never waive a financing condition on a term sheet.
I know which conditions precedent are objective and which are discretionary.
I asked for the material adverse change clause to exclude general market changes.
Every covenant breach has notice and a cure period before default.
Cross-default is limited to the same borrower and a meaningful threshold.
I know how security will be registered and enforced where the property sits.
A lawyer in the governing law reviews the commitment letter before I sign.
head: Field checklist
speak: A lender’s yes comes in three stages. The term sheet is usually non-binding on the loan itself, though it may bind me on fees or exclusivity. The commitment letter is a binding offer subject to conditions precedent, and I read each one asking who decides it and whether that decision is objective. A condition the lender must be satisfied with in its sole discretion is close to an option for the lender. I narrow the material adverse change clause to the borrower and property, not the market. Once funded, the loan agreement binds me through covenants; I want notice and a cure period, and I limit cross-default so one building’s trouble does not spread to every loan. Canada and Guyana both protect lenders through registered security, though the systems differ. And I never waive my own financing condition until the lender’s remaining conditions are objective and within my control.
terms: Commitment letter — a lender’s binding offer to lend on stated terms, subject to conditions precedent.
Material adverse change clause — a clause letting a lender refuse to fund if something seriously harms the borrower, the property or the market, as defined.
Cross-default — a clause making a default under another loan an event of default under this one.

hostile.q: Our commitment letter is standard. Why does your lawyer want to change the material adverse change clause?
hostile.a: Because as drafted it lets you refuse to fund if the general market weakens, which is precisely the moment we will need the money. We are happy for it to cover a serious change in our own condition or in the property, which is the risk you are really underwriting. If market risk is a concern, we would rather discuss a lower loan amount now than an uncertain one later.

title: Sizing the Loan, Testing the Headroom, Finding the Walk-Away
summary: Priya sizes a hypothetical loan under three lender limits, finds the one that binds, tests covenant headroom and rate sensitivity, and shows when a larger offer is a trap and when the right answer is to walk away. All numbers are hypothetical and rounded.
body:
How much a lender will lend is set by whichever of its tests bites first. Find that number, then ask how far income can fall before the covenant breaks, and you will know whether to take the loan, trade for a better one or walk away.

Recall

Q. What is a cash sweep?

A. A clause that diverts surplus cash to the lender when a test such as the coverage ratio falls below a set level, either to pay down the loan or to hold in reserve.

Q. At a checkpoint, how do you compute the cash that reaches an owner through a structure?

A. Start with distributable cash at the project, then subtract tax, withholding and costs at each layer on the way up, in order.

Q. What is the first step in deciding whether foreign-affiliate income is taxed currently?

A. Classify it: active business income or passive income, using the definitions in the owner’s country, which you verify against the primary source.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the numbers behind every lender conversation are the same few calculations. If you can do them on one page, you can sit with a lender as an equal, spot a bigger offer that is really a trap, and know in advance the point at which you walk away.

The building and the limits

All figures are hypothetical. A stabilised building earns net operating income (NOI) of 2,000,000 dollars a year. The lender’s terms: maximum debt service coverage ratio (DSCR) of 1.25 at closing; maximum loan to value (LTV) of 65 percent; minimum debt yield, meaning NOI divided by loan amount, of 9 percent. The rate is 6.5 percent with payments over a 25-year amortisation. The appraiser values the building at a 6 percent cap rate.

Step 1: size the loan under each limit

Coverage first. At 1.25, debt service can be at most 2,000,000 divided by 1.25, which is 1,600,000 dollars a year. The annual payment on each dollar borrowed at 6.5 percent over 25 years, called the loan constant, is about 0.081. So the loan can be at most 1,600,000 divided by 0.081, about 19,750,000 dollars.

Value second. At a 6 percent cap rate the building is worth 2,000,000 divided by 0.06, about 33,330,000 dollars. Sixty-five percent of that is about 21,670,000 dollars.

Debt yield third. At 9 percent, the loan can be at most 2,000,000 divided by 0.09, about 22,220,000 dollars.

The smallest of the three binds. Here coverage binds at about 19,750,000 dollars. That is the loan.

Say that out loud now.

Step 2: test the covenant headroom

Suppose the loan agreement adds an ongoing covenant: coverage must stay above 1.15, tested quarterly. With debt service of 1,600,000 dollars, the NOI floor is 1.15 times 1,600,000, which is 1,840,000 dollars. NOI can fall from 2,000,000 to 1,840,000 dollars, about 8 percent, before you breach. Ask yourself whether 8 percent is enough for this building, given its tenants, its expenses and its market. If one tenant is 10 percent of income, it is not.

Step 3: test the rate

If the rate were 7 percent instead of 6.5 percent, the loan constant rises to about 0.085, and the coverage-sized loan falls to 1,600,000 divided by 0.085, about 18,860,000 dollars. A half-point rise between term sheet and closing cuts the loan by nearly 900,000 dollars. If your rate is floating, the same rise after closing eats into your headroom instead. That is the arithmetic behind Ford’s case on Day 2.

A second worked example: the bigger offer that is a trap

A second lender offers 21,500,000 dollars at the same 6.5 percent, with the same 1.15 ongoing covenant. Debt service would be about 21,500,000 times 0.081, roughly 1,742,000 dollars. Coverage at closing would be 2,000,000 divided by 1,742,000, about 1.15. You would be at the covenant on the day you close, with no headroom at all. The extra 1,750,000 dollars is not extra money; it is a default waiting for its first bad month. The only ways to make it safe are an interest-only period, a funded reserve, or a lower covenant, and each has a price.

Step 4: find the walk-away

Suppose total project cost is 30,000,000 dollars. With a 19,750,000 dollar loan, equity needed is 10,250,000 dollars. If you have commitments for 10,000,000 dollars, you are 250,000 dollars short. Your options, in order of preference: raise 250,000 dollars more equity; cut cost by 250,000 dollars; negotiate a slightly larger loan with real headroom, perhaps through a longer amortisation, which lowers the constant. If none is available, the honest answer is to walk away or restructure, not to take the 21,500,000 dollar loan.

A third worked example: longer amortisation

Suppose the lender agrees to a 30-year amortisation instead of 25 years at the same 6.5 percent. The loan constant falls from about 0.081 to about 0.076. The coverage-sized loan becomes 1,600,000 divided by 0.076, about 21,050,000 dollars. That closes the 250,000 dollar equity gap with room to spare. But check the other limits: 65 percent loan to value allows about 21,670,000 dollars and the 9 percent debt yield about 22,220,000 dollars, so neither binds yet. Then check the cost: the loan pays down more slowly, so at refinancing in year five you will owe more than you would have on a 25-year schedule. That is acceptable only if your exit plan allows for a larger balance.

A sensible borrower would not take the full 21,050,000 dollars. He would borrow what closes the gap, about 20,000,000 dollars, keep the coverage at about 1.32 on the longer schedule, and keep the headroom. Debt service on 20,000,000 dollars at a 0.076 constant is about 1,520,000 dollars, so the NOI floor under the 1.15 covenant is about 1,748,000 dollars, a fall of about 12.6 percent. Borrowing less than the maximum is how you buy headroom.

Put it on one page

A lender-ready page lists: NOI, each sizing limit and the loan it allows, the binding limit, coverage at closing, the NOI floor and percentage headroom, the rate sensitivity, the equity required and the source of every dollar of it. If you can produce that page in an hour, you can hold your own in any lender meeting.

When to stop asking for more

There is a point at which every extra dollar of loan costs more than it is worth. Each dollar beyond the coverage-sized amount lowers your headroom, raises the chance of a sweep and increases any recourse you carry. A useful test: after each increase, recompute the NOI floor and ask whether the building could survive losing its largest tenant. If the answer turns from yes to no, you have found your borrowing limit, and it is often below the lender’s. Write that limit down next to your walk-away so the conversation with the lender starts from your number, not theirs.

Do this arithmetic before the first lender call, not after the term sheet arrives.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is taking the largest loan offered because it closes the equity gap, without checking headroom. The control: compute coverage at closing and the NOI floor under the ongoing covenant for every offer, and reject any loan that sits at its covenant on day one.

The beginner's mistake

Computing only the loan to value limit, which is usually the most generous, and being surprised when the lender sizes on coverage.

Callback

In Week 36, Priya taught the four sizing tests. Today added the second half of the job: once the loan is sized, test how far income and rates can move before it breaks, and decide your walk-away before the lender asks you to sign.

Recap

Size under every limit and take the smallest. Test headroom as a percentage fall in NOI. Test the rate. Reject any loan that starts at its covenant. If the gap cannot be filled honestly, walk.

Next: Priya on The Room: the call where the lender re-trades the deal.
checklist: I sized the loan under coverage, loan to value and debt yield.
I know which limit binds and by how much.
I computed the NOI floor under the ongoing covenant.
I tested the loan size against a half-point rate rise.
I checked coverage at closing for every larger offer.
I know my equity gap and the options to close it.
I decided my walk-away before the lender asked me to sign.
head: Field checklist
speak: With NOI of 2,000,000 dollars, a 1.25 coverage test allows 1,600,000 dollars of debt service, which at 6.5 percent over 25 years is a loan of about 19,750,000 dollars. Sixty-five percent loan to value would allow about 21,670,000 dollars and a 9 percent debt yield about 22,220,000 dollars, so coverage binds. With an ongoing covenant of 1.15, NOI can fall to 1,840,000 dollars, about 8 percent, before a breach. A half-point rate rise cuts the loan by almost 900,000 dollars. A second lender offering 21,500,000 dollars would put coverage at 1.15 on closing day, so that offer is a trap. With a 30,000,000 dollar project and 10,000,000 dollars of equity, I am 250,000 dollars short. I close it with equity, cost or a safer longer amortisation, or I walk.
terms: Loan constant — the annual payment, interest plus principal, per dollar borrowed at a given rate and amortisation.
Debt yield — net operating income divided by the loan amount, a sizing test that ignores the rate.
NOI floor — the lowest net operating income at which a coverage covenant is still met.

hostile.q: We can lend you 21,500,000 dollars. Why are you asking for less?
hostile.a: Because at that amount coverage is about 1.15 on closing day, exactly at your covenant, so any dip in income puts us in default. I would rather borrow about 19,750,000 dollars with 8 percent of headroom. If you want to lend more, I would discuss an interest-only period or a funded reserve, priced properly, but I will not sign a loan that is at its limit on day one.

title: When the Lender Re-Trades the Deal
summary: Two weeks before closing, the lender calls: the credit committee wants a higher coverage ratio and full recourse. Priya gives the lines to say, the lines never to say, the question behind the question and how to hold your state, plus this month’s thread on working with advisers.
body:
A late re-trade is a test of your alternatives, not of your temper. If you kept a second lender warm and know your walk-away, you can stay calm, ask the right question and trade back. If you did not, you will pay whatever the committee asks.

Recall

Q. What does Rule 67 say?

A. Never trade structure for price until you have priced the downside; a lower rate is not worth wider recourse, a tighter covenant or an unhedged floating rate unless its saving is larger than the expected cost of the bad case.

Q. In a checkpoint mock meeting with a banker, what does the banker want first?

A. The bottom line: how much cash reaches the borrower, where it can be trapped and what security the bank holds.

Q. When advising on a foreign affiliate in a meeting, what should you never do?

A. Never give a conclusion on how its income is taxed without a qualified adviser’s view on the specific facts and the rules that apply.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a re-trade, meaning a counterparty reopening agreed terms late in a deal, is one of the most common and most stressful moments in development finance. It usually comes when you have already spent money, set a land closing date and told your investors. That timing is not an accident. Your leverage is lowest when you have committed the most. Today you practise the call.

The scene

All figures are hypothetical. Two weeks before closing, the lender’s relationship manager calls. The agreed terms were a 19,750,000 dollar loan, a 1.25 coverage ratio at closing and recourse capped at 5,000,000 dollars. He says: “Credit committee has looked again. They want 1.35 coverage, which brings the loan to about 18,300,000, and they want full recourse. I am sorry, my hands are tied.” Your commitment letter contained a market-flex clause, which lets the lender change pricing or structure if market conditions shift before closing, within stated limits.

The question behind the question

Behind the committee’s demand is a question: has the risk changed, or has our appetite changed? If something about your building has changed, such as a tenant leaving or a cost rising, you need to know. If the bank’s own portfolio or the market has changed, you are being asked to pay for the lender’s problem. And behind the relationship manager’s apology is another question: will you make his life easy or hard with his committee? He is not your enemy. He may be your best advocate if you give him something to take back.

The lines to say

Start by understanding. “Thank you for telling me early. Can you help me understand what changed: something about our building, or the committee’s view of the market?”

Then go to the document. “Our commitment letter has a market-flex clause. Can we look together at what it allows and whether this change is within it?”

Then offer a trade instead of a refusal. “We cannot accept full recourse. We could accept 1.30 coverage with the existing cap, or keep 1.25 and fund an interest reserve of six months. Which would help most with your committee?”

And state your alternative calmly, if you have one. “I need to be transparent: we have kept a second lender informed, and I will need to speak with them by Friday if we cannot find a path.”

Say that out loud now.

The lines never to say

Never say, “We have no other options,” even if it is true. Never threaten to complain to his manager on the first call. Never agree to full recourse on the phone to keep the closing date. Never invent a competing lender; that is a misrepresentation, and lenders talk to each other more than borrowers think. And never say, “That is fine” about anything until you have priced it.

When to stay silent

Stay silent after you ask what changed. Let him explain fully; the details he gives are your best evidence of whether this is about your building. Stay silent again after you propose your trade. Then end the call with a time: “Can we speak again on Wednesday at ten?”

Holding your state

A re-trade feels like a betrayal, and the feeling pushes you to fight or to give in. Do neither on the first call. Take notes, ask questions, and say you will come back. After the call, while parked or at your desk, slow your breathing if that helps, then price the demand: full recourse adds 14,750,000 dollars of exposure; the smaller loan opens a gap of about 1,450,000 dollars. You cannot decide well until you know those numbers.

A worked example of the trade

By Wednesday you have priced the options. Accepting 1.30 coverage reduces the loan to about 19,000,000 dollars, a gap of 750,000 dollars, which your investors can fill. Funding a six-month interest reserve would cost about 640,000 dollars of borrowed money. You offer 1.30 coverage, the existing 5,000,000 dollar recourse cap and monthly reporting. The committee accepts, because its real concern was coverage, not recourse. You close a week late with your downside intact.

Working with advisers

This month’s thread is working with advisers. In a re-trade, you need three people quickly: your own lawyer to read the market-flex clause, a mortgage broker or financing adviser who knows what other lenders are doing this month, and your accountant to price the changes. Brief them before you need them, so that a Wednesday deadline is not their first sight of the deal.

Remember whose side each adviser is on. The lender’s counsel works for the lender even though you may pay the bill. A broker paid only on closing has an incentive to close; ask how they are paid. Your job is to use each adviser for what they do best, and to make the decision yourself.

What the relationship manager writes after the call

After your call, the relationship manager writes a note for his committee. You want that note to say three things: the borrower asked what changed and understood the concern; the borrower proposed a reasonable, priced alternative; and the borrower has another lender, so delay carries a risk of losing the deal. You influence each of those sentences by what you said and how you said it. Send him a short email the same day confirming your proposal, with the numbers, so he can paste it straight into his note. Make it easy for your advocate to advocate.

If there is no second lender

Sometimes there genuinely is no alternative ready. Then do not pretend otherwise, and do not tell the lender so. Ask for time instead: “We need until Friday to consider this properly with our investors.” Use that time to call two other lenders and ask whether they could close quickly on the existing terms. Even a slower alternative changes your position, because it means a late re-trade risks losing the deal rather than merely delaying it. And next time, start the second conversation earlier.

The lesson is that alternatives are built in advance and cannot be invented on the day.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is conceding under time pressure because you have no alternative. The control is to keep a second lender informed until closing and to price every change before you answer it.

The beginner's mistake

Arguing about fairness instead of asking what changed. The answer to that question tells you what trade will work.

Callback

In Week 66, JAX and Kema taught that your alternative does more negotiating than anything you say. A re-trade is where that becomes literal: the second lender you kept warm is the only reason the first one negotiates at all.

Recap

Ask what changed, read the market-flex clause, propose a priced trade, state your alternative calmly, and never concede on the first call. Brief your advisers early and know who each one works for.

Next: Kema on Quiz and Recap: Week 67 review.
checklist: I kept a second lender informed until closing.
I asked whether the risk or the lender’s appetite had changed.
I read the market-flex clause before responding.
I priced every requested change before answering.
I offered a trade instead of a refusal.
I did not concede anything on the first call.
My lawyer, broker and accountant were briefed before the deadline.
I know how each adviser is paid and whose side each is on.
head: Field checklist
speak: Two weeks before closing, the lender asks for 1.35 coverage and full recourse. On the first call I do not fight and I do not give in. I thank him for telling me early and ask what changed: something about our building, or the committee’s view of the market. I stay silent while he explains. Then I go to the commitment letter’s market-flex clause and ask whether this change is within it. I propose a priced trade instead of a refusal, for example 1.30 coverage with the existing recourse cap, and I mention calmly that a second lender has been kept informed. I never claim I have no options, never invent a competitor and never agree to full recourse on the phone. Afterwards I price everything with my lawyer, broker and accountant. In this case, the committee’s real concern was coverage, so 1.30 with monthly reporting closed the deal with my downside intact.
terms: Re-trade — a counterparty reopening agreed terms late in a deal, usually when the other side has committed the most.
Market-flex clause — a clause letting a lender change pricing or structure before closing if market conditions shift, within stated limits.
Relationship manager — the lender’s main contact for a borrower, who must persuade the lender’s credit committee.

hostile.q: If you cannot accept the committee’s terms, we will have to withdraw. Are you prepared for that?
hostile.a: I would rather not, and I do not think you would either, given the work we have both done. I am prepared to accept 1.30 coverage and monthly reporting, which addresses the change in your committee’s view of coverage. I cannot accept full recourse. If that is a firm requirement, then yes, we will speak to the other lender, and I would ask you to tell me by Wednesday so we both have time.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 67 Review: What to Ask For, What to Trade, When to Walk
summary: Six questions on negotiating with lenders, a recap of the week, a Red Pen drill on a flawed term-sheet summary, and a two-minute boardroom explanation. Answer each question aloud before you read the answer.
body:
This week came down to one sentence: negotiate a loan’s structure before its price, turn every term into dollars, and keep an alternative alive until the money arrives.

Recall

Q. How do you compare two loans with different fees and rates on price alone?

A. Spread each upfront fee over the expected hold period and add it to the rate to get the all-in rate, then compare.

Q. What should you record from a checkpoint recording session?

A. Your score from 1 to 5 for accuracy, structure, composure and the hard question, and the single point to fix before the next recording.

Q. In concept, why does a controlled-foreign-company rule exist?

A. To stop residents deferring tax by keeping passive or mobile income in a foreign company they control. The rules vary; verify against the primary source.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, you will negotiate with lenders more often than with almost anyone else in your career, and the terms you accept will decide how your projects behave in a bad year. If you can answer these six questions without notes, you are ready for a lender meeting. Answer each aloud first.

The six questions

Question 1. What is the difference between a loan’s price terms and its structure terms?

Answer: Price terms are the rate, fees and hedge costs: what the loan costs when things go to plan. Structure terms are size, recourse, covenants, reserves, cash management, prepayment and conditions: what the loan does to you when things go wrong.

Question 2. State Rule 67.

Answer: Never trade structure for price until you have priced the downside.

Question 3. How do you price a recourse difference between two offers?

Answer: Extra exposure times the chance of a call times the loss if called. For 15,000,000 dollars, a 3 percent chance and a 40 percent loss, about 180,000 dollars.

Question 4. Why should you not waive a financing condition on a term sheet?

Answer: Because a term sheet usually does not bind the lender to lend, so you could be bound to buy land with no committed loan.

Question 5. NOI is 2,000,000 dollars and debt service is 1,600,000 dollars. The covenant is 1.15. What is the NOI floor and the headroom?

Answer: The floor is 1,840,000 dollars, so NOI can fall about 8 percent before a breach.

Question 6. On a late re-trade, what is the first question to ask?

Answer: What changed: something about our building, or the lender’s view of the market. The answer tells you what trade will work.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

Priya split loans into price and structure and set out what to ask for, what to trade and when to walk. Ford and Roman took a composite case in which a cheaper loan with full recourse and a tight covenant cost a family its home, giving Rule 67. Roman priced every term in dollars. LEX explained what term sheets, commitment letters and loan agreements bind, with a Two Systems look at lender security in Canada and Guyana. Priya sized a loan and tested its headroom. Priya then ran the re-trade call.

Red Pen drill

Read this hypothetical memo summarising a term sheet, and find the defects before reading on.

Memo to partners. Great news: Lender C has offered the lowest rate we have seen, 0.40 percent below the others, on a 21,500,000 dollar loan, which closes our equity gap. Covenant DSCR 1.15 tested quarterly; our closing DSCR will be about 1.15. Rate is floating, so we save money if rates fall. Recourse is full, but the lender says it is standard and they never call it. Term sheet received and signed, so I have waived the financing condition on the land purchase. Prepayment premium is a formula; we will deal with it if we sell.

The defects. First, the memo leads with rate and ignores structure, the opposite of this week’s rule. Second, a 1.15 covenant against 1.15 coverage at closing means no headroom; the loan starts at its limit. Third, a floating rate is presented as upside only, with no cap or hedge quoted, so the downside is unpriced. Fourth, full recourse is accepted on the lender’s say-so that it is never called; a guarantee exists precisely to be called. Fifth, waiving the financing condition on a signed term sheet binds us to the land with no committed loan. Sixth, the prepayment formula is not modelled, though a sale in the first years could make it the largest cost in the loan.

Now rewrite the memo in your head: a comparison grid, price and structure in dollars, headroom stated as a percentage, a hedge quote, capped recourse, the financing condition kept, and the prepayment premium modelled at the likely sale dates.

The boardroom drill

Explain the week in two minutes, as if to an investor who asks, “How do you choose a lender?” Then compare with this model.

Model answer: “We invite several lenders to bid and put every term into one grid, price and structure side by side. We negotiate structure first: capped recourse with an end date, covenants with real headroom and a cure right, a sweep that switches off, and prepayment that fits our exit. We convert every term into dollars, fees over the expected hold, recourse and prepayment as expected costs, so we choose the cheapest loan in a bad year, not the lowest rate. We size the loan under every limit, take the smallest, and reject any offer that starts at its covenant. We keep our own financing condition until the lender’s conditions are objective, and we keep a second lender warm until we close. If the gap cannot be filled honestly, we walk.”

Score yourself. Did you lead with the bottom line? Did you mention structure before price? Did you put a number on recourse? Did you finish in two minutes?

How to use this review

Do not read the six answers and move on. Pick the one you found hardest and do the calculation again tomorrow with different numbers: change the NOI, the rate or the covenant and work out the headroom from scratch. Then take a real term sheet, from a past deal or a public example, and fill in the grid line by line, pricing each structure term. The first time takes an hour. The fifth time takes ten minutes, and by then you will see the expensive terms in a lender’s first draft before you finish reading it.

Finally, practise the re-trade call aloud with a friend playing the lender. Ask them to be unreasonable. Your aim is not to win the role-play; it is to hear yourself ask what changed, stay silent, and offer a priced trade without raising your voice.

Score each practice call from 1 to 5 on composure and on whether you priced the trade. Two points of improvement in a month is a real gain.

Keep the scores in your decision journal beside the date, so that you can see the trend over a season rather than judging yourself on a single bad session.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is choosing a loan on rate and discovering its structure in a downturn. The control is the grid, priced in dollars, and Rule 67.

The beginner's mistake

Signing the first term sheet because it arrived first. The second and third bids are what make the first one honest.

Callback

In Week 6, Kema taught the hostile question: acknowledge, bridge, answer. Every lender call this week used it. When the committee pushes, you acknowledge their concern, bridge to the document or the numbers, and answer with a priced trade.

Recap

Structure before price, every term in dollars, sizing under every limit, headroom as a percentage, conditions read for discretion, and an alternative kept alive. Rule 67 protects your household from a cheaper loan.

head: The six questions
speak: This week was about lenders. A loan has price terms, the rate and fees, and structure terms: size, recourse, covenants, reserves, sweeps, prepayment and conditions. Price matters in a good year; structure decides whether I survive a bad one, so I negotiate structure first. I turn every term into dollars: fees spread over the expected hold, recourse and prepayment as expected costs. Often the higher-rate loan is cheaper. I size under coverage, value and debt yield, take the smallest, and reject any offer that starts at its covenant. I know a term sheet rarely binds the lender, so I keep my financing condition until the remaining conditions are objective. When a lender re-trades, I ask what changed, read the market-flex clause and offer a priced trade, with a second lender kept warm. Rule 67: never trade structure for price until I have priced the downside.
terms: Comparison grid — a single table setting every lender’s price and structure terms side by side.
Headroom — the margin between current performance and a covenant level, best stated as a percentage fall in income.
Second lender — an alternative lender kept informed until closing so the first one negotiates in good faith.

hostile.q: An investor asks: if rates rise two percentage points next year, what happens to your loan?
hostile.a: Our loan is fixed for five years, so debt service does not change. Coverage stays at about 1.25 against a 1.15 covenant, so income can fall about 8 percent before a breach. At refinancing, a two-point rise would reduce the loan we could get, and we have modelled that and the equity it might need. Recourse is capped at 5,000,000 dollars and ends at stabilisation. I can send you the sensitivity table.
